description: We're two second-semester engineering students (Systems and Engineering) who have been building projects together since high school. We love turning information into creative solutions: what we don't know, we learn or invent. I focus on product structure and leveraging AI; my teammate leads communication and relationships. We joined to test our skills on a real challenge, experiment, and keep learning. We'd love teammates who are curious, proactive, and eager to build.
summary:
Starlight Journey is an interactive, bilingual (English and Spanish) website that turns the history of space exploration into an adventure. Users play a "Commander" who travels from Earth to the Moon and Mars to find five NASA artifacts: the Apollo Lunar Module, Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, and Ingenuity. Each one can be rotated and taken apart in 3D, piece by piece, to discover what it did. Exploring every part unlocks the full report and a quiz, with an explanation whenever an answer is wrong. A voice narration accompanies the journey.
We want children and young people to learn out of curiosity, not just by reading. It matters because it sparks interest in science and engineering, and shows that behind every mission were people who dared to ask questions. The information is based on NASA sources.
details:
What it does and how it works. Starlight Journey is an interactive, bilingual (English/Spanish) website where users play a "Commander" who flies from Earth to the Moon and Mars to explore five NASA artifacts: the Apollo Lunar Module, Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity. Each artifact is a 3D model that can be rotated and taken apart piece by piece with a slider. Tapping a part opens a card explaining it. After exploring every part, the full report unlocks (mission facts, legacy and detail on each part), followed by a 3-question challenge drawn at random, with an explanation when an answer is wrong. Voice narration, with text that lights up as it plays, tells the story of the start, the Moon, Mars and the final "Mission accomplished" screen.

Benefits and intended impact. It lets children and young people learn space history by exploring instead of only reading, and it spark curiosity about science and engineering. Because it runs in any browser, in two languages, and on phone or computer, it is easy to reach and easy to share.

Tools used. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules); three.js with its GLTF, Draco and OrbitControls add-ons for 3D; GLB models from NASA 3D Resources; WebP images and MP3 audio; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting (no server needed). AI tools: Claude (coding, 3D model integration and help with texts), ChatGPT and Gemini (illustrations), ElevenLabs (narration voices).

Creativity. Instead of a static fact sheet, the project is a story: the user is an astronaut, the artifacts are "stations", and each model opens up like an exploded view. Learning is tied to play through unlockable reports, a quiz, points and badges, and a finale.

Factors we considered. Accuracy first: every fact comes from NASA or JPL pages, and anything uncertain was removed. Language suited to young readers, plus full English and Spanish versions. Accessibility and comfort: mute and skip buttons, readable text that follows the audio, and a layout that works on phones. Technical limits: free hosting, file sizes, and the 3D models, whose parts we split by hand, so some groupings are approximate. Honesty about AI: the illustrations are artistic, not real photographs, and all AI use is credited in the project
